7-1.title: Minerals
7-1.learn:
KEY IDEAS

A mineral is a naturally formed SOLID with a specific chemical makeup and an orderly CRYSTAL pattern inside. (Minerals are not made by living things and are not man-made.)

Scientists identify minerals by their PROPERTIES:
- Color: what color it appears (but color alone can be misleading).
- Hardness: how easily it can be scratched (measured on the Mohs scale).
- Luster: how shiny or dull it looks (metallic vs. nonmetallic).
- Streak: the color of the powder it leaves when scraped on a tile.

Minerals are the building blocks of ROCKS, and we use them in everyday items.

Example 1 — Streak vs. color
Two minerals may look the same color, but their STREAK (powder color) can be different, helping tell them apart.

Example 2 — Hardness test
A harder mineral can scratch a softer one. Diamond is the hardest mineral, so it can scratch nearly anything.

Example 3 — Is it a mineral?
A salt crystal is a mineral (natural solid, orderly crystal pattern). Sugar from a plant or a plastic bead is NOT a mineral, because minerals must form naturally and not from living things.

7-2.title: Rocks and How They Form
7-2.learn:
KEY IDEAS

Rocks are made of one or more minerals. There are three main types, grouped by how they form:
- Igneous rock forms when melted rock (magma or lava) COOLS and hardens. (Example: granite, basalt.)
- Sedimentary rock forms when bits of rock and sand get PRESSED and CEMENTED together in layers. (Example: sandstone, limestone.)
- Metamorphic rock forms when HEAT and PRESSURE change an existing rock WITHOUT melting it. (Example: marble from limestone, slate from shale.)

The type of rock tells a story about how and where it formed.

Example 1 — Cooled lava
When lava from a volcano cools and hardens, it forms igneous rock.

Example 2 — Layers at the bottom of a lake
Sand and mud settle in layers, then get pressed and cemented into sedimentary rock.

Example 3 — Squeezed and heated
When limestone is heated and squeezed deep underground (without melting), it becomes the metamorphic rock marble.

7-3.title: The Rock Cycle
7-3.learn:
KEY IDEAS

The rock cycle is the never-ending loop in which rocks slowly change from one type to another over millions of years. Any rock can become any other type.

Main processes that change rocks:
- Heat and pressure → turn rock into METAMORPHIC rock.
- Melting → turns rock into magma, which cools into IGNEOUS rock.
- Weathering and erosion → break rock into sediment, which gets pressed into SEDIMENTARY rock.

Example 1 — Igneous to sedimentary
An igneous rock can be weathered into tiny pieces (sediment), which are then pressed and cemented into sedimentary rock.

Example 2 — Any to igneous
Any rock that gets hot enough to MELT becomes magma; when it cools, it forms igneous rock.

Example 3 — Slow change
The rock cycle takes a very long time — usually millions of years — as rocks melt, break down, or get squeezed into new forms.
